chapter: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
title: How Duke wrote for individual players
summary: Ellington gave each man particular notes in chords and made new arrangements when personnel changed; he used Hamilton, Procope and Carney expertly.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: And I noticed how he would use different musicians in the band. He would take your sound and use it. He would give you certain notes and certain chords, like he would give me certain notes in a chord that he wouldn't give Lawrence or give Tyree or even Britt Woodman or John Sanders, and that's the way he wrote, you see? And that's the reason that he had a lot of different arrangements on one tune in a book. If there was a change in the personnel of the band, that arrangement wouldn't sound the same to him, so he would make a new one, you see.

That's right. And he knew how to use every one. He had two great clarinet players in the band. He had Jimmy Hamilton and Russell Procope. He knew just how to use them. He knew how to use Harry Carney on that baritone saxophone. I have watched different arrangements that sometimes Carney would be playing up above the tenor, even, and then all at once when he wanted a big drop he'd -- Bam -- he'd drop it right down and make that whole chord just fall down like a big rock hit the bottom of the ground, you know?
Yeah. So you'd call him a musical chemist, more or less, eh?
He'd mix sounds like you mix --
